newsitem.title: GERMANY: German DAX ends bourse mixed, dollar weighs.
newsitem.headline: German DAX ends bourse mixed, dollar weighs.

text.p: The German share market clawed back early dollar-led losses to end bourse trade just ahead on Monday, as worries about U.S. rate rises and the fate of Europe's monetary union added to price volatility.
The 30-share DAX, having hit a low of 3,306.15 points in the pre-bourse IBIS electronic phase, closed the bourse session up 3.19 points, or 0.10 percent at 3,347.58.
Gains and losses were fairly evenly spread and deealers said the market was strongly driven by technical factors, with solid investment interest notably lacking.
"Customers don't have the nerve to buy at the moment. There simply isn't anything to drive interest from the home side," said a Frankfurt trader.
The dollar's slide against the mark weighed on prices from the start and drove Daimler-Benz to sharp losses as it added to worries about an imminent hike in German fuel prices.

Daimler dropped 3.20 marks, or 2.4 percent, to 128.30 marks in bourse trade after Germany's mass circulation Bild newspaper said the government planned a sharp increase in petrol tax before the summer. Chancellor Helmut Kohl later denied having any such plans.
Daimler's losses were offset by a strong performance by software group SAP and engineering giant Siemens.
Ahead of its first quarter earnings report due on Tuesday, SAP preferred stock rose 8.20 marks to 292.90 marks.
Siemens, due to report first half earnings this week, rose 1.35 marks to 90 marks.

Sports retail group Puma took a sharp dive on concerns about weak output outlook, triggered by news earlier this month from U.S. rival Nike that it was reducing production capacity. Puma's shares ended bourse trade down 2.80 marks at 57 marks.
There were few general market moving factors about. German March M3 money supply came in as expected at an annualised rate of 8.3 percent and thus had minimal market impact.
But dealers said talk had re-emerged about the problems facing Europe's single currency project, which was contributing to overall market angst.
